Chapter Two: Redefining Success—From Fixing Problems to Managing Them
Let’s talk about a shift that can really change the way you approach challenges. Most of us have been taught to believe that every problem can be solved, right? If you just work hard enough, or say the right thing, you’ll find that one magic solution.
But if you’ve ever wrestled with a tough family relationship, ongoing sadness, or the ups and downs of daily life, you know—some struggles don’t just disappear. They’re not puzzles you solve once and never see again.
Here’s something important: There’s a big difference between fixing and managing. Management is about sticking with it, making adjustments, and giving things the care they need—over and over.
Think of it like tending a garden. No matter how many weeds you pull, a few are bound to pop up again. The weather changes, the seasons shift, and you can’t control everything. The goal isn’t a perfect yard; it’s to keep things healthy and as peaceful as they can be.
So, how does this way of thinking play out in real life? Let’s look at a few examples.
Maybe you’ve got a family member who always stirs up drama. You’ve tried talking, you’ve tried helping, but nothing really changes. Instead of chasing that perfect fix, it can help to focus on setting boundaries and managing how you interact with them.
Or, take chronic emotional pain—grief, anxiety, anger. These feelings might fade for a while, but they often come back. The real task isn’t to erase them, but to learn how to live alongside them, so they don’t take over your whole life.
And then there’s the reality that life just isn’t fair sometimes. No matter how hard you push, some obstacles aren’t going away. Managing means finding ways to cope, adapt, and move forward, even when things aren’t right.
So, what does a management mindset actually look like day-to-day?
First, set realistic expectations. Some problems stick around, and progress can be slow or bumpy.
Next, prioritize your energy. Put your focus where it can actually make a difference, instead of burning out on things you just can’t control.
And, build routines. Habits and boundaries can help you keep things together, even when feelings or circumstances are tough.
Imagine someone whose partner struggles with addiction. They might wish for an overnight fix, but the truth is, change takes time—and sometimes it doesn’t come at all. Instead of trying to force that transformation, they might focus on their own boundaries, reach out for support, and protect their own well-being.
When you shift your definition of success from “I have to fix this” to “I’m managing as best I can,” you take a huge weight off your shoulders. You stop blaming yourself. You stop feeling disappointed when things aren’t perfect.
Life is messy. But if you’re doing your best, even when things aren’t ideal, that’s a success worth celebrating.
